body:
Why a large military establishment was necessary

The Delhi Sultans needed armies to defend the capital, suppress rebellions, enforce provincial authority and conduct campaigns. The cavalry was particularly important because mounted soldiers could move quickly and undertake operations across large distances.

Armies also included infantry, war elephants and specialists involved in fortification, transport and siege warfare. Their numbers and relative importance differed between campaigns.

Military organisation and payment

The Sultan could command troops directly and require military service from provincial commanders. A muqti maintained soldiers from the authorised revenue of his iqta. However, some Sultans also maintained large bodies of centrally paid soldiers.

Maintaining a standing army meant providing soldiers with regular pay, food, horses and equipment even when no campaign was taking place. A ruler therefore needed reliable revenue and a system for checking whether the soldiers and horses recorded on the rolls actually existed.

Alauddin Khalji's military measures

The Mongol threat intensified during Alauddin Khalji's reign. Attacks on Delhi and its surrounding territories, particularly around 1299–1303, made defensive preparations essential.

Alauddin strengthened his army and built Siri as a new garrison town near Delhi. He preferred cash salaries for his centrally maintained soldiers. Regular cash payment allowed the soldiers to purchase supplies, but it also made market prices an important military concern.

Dagh: branding of horses

Dagh was the practice of marking or branding horses for identification. It helped prevent a commander from presenting the same horse repeatedly during inspection or substituting an inferior animal for a better one recorded in military service.

Hulya or chehra: description of soldiers

A descriptive record of individual soldiers, commonly discussed under the terms hulya or chehra, helped officials identify the men on the military rolls.

Horse identification and soldier identification served different purposes. Both were useful in preventing false musters and the misuse of military funds.

Role of the Diwan-i-Arz

The Diwan-i-Arz was concerned with military administration, including the organisation and inspection of troops. Its associated senior officer was the ariz-i-mumalik. This administrative role supported the Sultan's military authority but was not identical to the position of a battlefield general.

How Mongol pressure shaped state policy

The connection between military threats and economic reforms was especially clear under Alauddin. To maintain a large force at manageable cost, he combined cash salaries with efforts to control the prices and supplies of essential goods in Delhi.

Muhammad bin Tughluq also maintained a large army, but his policies differed: he contemplated an offensive campaign towards Transoxiana, whereas Alauddin's principal military preparations against the Mongols were defensive.

Prelims focus

  • Siri: garrison town built by Alauddin Khalji.
  • Dagh: identification or branding of horses.
  • Hulya or chehra: descriptive identification of soldiers.
  • Diwan-i-Arz: military administration.
  • Alauddin paid his centrally maintained soldiers in cash.
  • Trap: Dagh identified horses, whereas hulya or chehra identified soldiers.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, Chapter 3, The Delhi Sultans, printed pp. 40–42, 2020–21 edition; IGNOU, eGyanKosh, Indian Polity: The Sultanate, Unit 16, sections on military administration and inspection, consulted 19 November 2026; NIOS, Senior Secondary History, Lesson 9, Establishment and Expansion of the Delhi Sultanate, sections on Alauddin Khalji's military measures, consulted 19 November 2026.]

title: The Sultanate Army, Cavalry and Military Reforms

body:
Why the Sultan regulated markets

Alauddin Khalji (1296–1316) maintained a large army to meet military threats, especially those posed by the Mongols. Soldiers received cash salaries and needed to buy food, clothing and other necessities.

If prices rose sharply, the Sultan would face pressure to increase military salaries. This could make a large standing army more expensive. Alauddin therefore introduced a system of state-regulated prices and supplies, particularly in Delhi.

Central relationship: Alauddin's market regulations were closely connected to maintaining a large cash-paid army at a controlled cost.

Goods covered by the regulations

The government regulated several categories of goods rather than restricting its attention to grain alone:

  • Food grains: essential for soldiers and the urban population.
  • Cloth and manufactured goods: important items of everyday consumption.
  • Horses and cattle: relevant to military needs, transport and the wider economy.
  • Other specified commodities: including certain valuable and luxury goods.

The Sarai-i-Adl was associated with the regulated market for cloth and other specified commodities. The grain market and markets for animals were subject to their own arrangements.

Officials who supervised the markets

Market supervision required information, inspections and penalties for violations. Important terms associated with Alauddin's arrangements include:

TermFunction
Diwan-i-RiyasatDepartment associated with the administration of market controls
Shahna-i-MandiMarket superintendent responsible for supervision
BaridOfficial reporting and intelligence duties
MunhiyanSecret informers reporting violations and market conditions

Merchants could be required to register and sell at prescribed rates. Officials checked prices, weights and supplies. Traders who violated the regulations could face penalties.

How the government tried to maintain supplies

Fixing a low price would be ineffective if goods disappeared from the market. The administration therefore also attempted to secure regular supplies.

Grain could be obtained through revenue collection and brought to markets by traders and transporters. Government grain stores helped provide reserves during shortages. Measures against hoarding sought to prevent merchants from withholding essential goods in expectation of higher prices.

Banjaras, who transported grain using pack animals and bullock caravans, played an important role in moving food to urban markets. Their caravans were known as tandas.

Results and limitations

Contemporary and later chroniclers described Alauddin's markets as having relatively stable and inexpensive supplies. However, such assessments came largely from accounts focused on the royal administration.

The regulations depended on strong enforcement, reliable supply and the authority of the ruler. They are best understood as an exceptional programme of intensive supervision, especially in Delhi and its regulated markets, rather than proof that the same prices were imposed uniformly across the entire subcontinent.

The policy also placed obligations on merchants, transporters and cultivators. Cheap urban supplies were not necessarily beneficial to every producer or trader.

Prelims focus

  • Alauddin Khalji: large standing army and market-price regulations.
  • Sarai-i-Adl: regulated market associated with cloth and other goods.
  • Shahna-i-Mandi: market superintendent.
  • Munhiyan: secret informers.
  • Banjaras: mobile transporters and traders; their caravans were called tandas.
  • Trap: The reforms were not confined to grain, and they were not a uniform all-India price system.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, Chapter 3, The Delhi Sultans, printed p. 41, and Chapter 7, Tribes, Nomads and Settled Communities, printed pp. 94–95, 2020–21 edition; IGNOU, eGyanKosh, Economy of the Delhi Sultanate, Unit 19, State and Economy, section on Alauddin Khalji's market regulations, consulted 19 November 2026.]

title: Alauddin Khalji's Market Regulations and Their Military Purpose

body:
A different approach to state expansion

Muhammad bin Tughluq, who ruled during the 14th century, attempted several ambitious administrative and military measures. Like Alauddin Khalji, he maintained a large army and sought to strengthen the Sultanate. However, he pursued different methods, and several measures encountered serious difficulties.

Military plans and the capital

After successfully resisting a Mongol attack, Muhammad bin Tughluq prepared for a possible campaign towards Transoxiana in Central Asia. This represented an offensive military ambition rather than merely the defence of Delhi against invading armies.

He also ordered a major transfer of administrative activity and sections of Delhi's population to Daulatabad, formerly Devagiri, in the Deccan. Daulatabad's location offered advantages for supervising southern territories, but the movement imposed great hardship on many residents.

The older Delhi settlement of Dehli-i-Kuhna was used for military accommodation. The attempted reorganisation contributed to discontent, and the arrangements did not produce the stable administrative results the Sultan sought.

The experiment with token currency

Muhammad bin Tughluq issued token coins made of cheaper metals, including copper and brass, intended to circulate at an officially assigned value comparable to the silver currency.

The underlying idea was that a coin's recognised purchasing power need not equal the market value of its metal. For such a system to function, however, people must trust the currency and the state must control its issue.

Counterfeiting became a major problem. People could produce imitations of the lower-value metal coins, while retaining gold and silver. The government faced difficulty distinguishing genuine issues from imitations and eventually withdrew the token currency.

Important distinction: The experiment did not fail simply because the coins were made of copper or brass. The serious difficulties included counterfeiting, inadequate control and loss of confidence in the currency.

Taxation and distress in the Ganga–Yamuna Doab

The Ganga–Yamuna Doab, the tract between the 2 rivers, was an important agricultural region supplying revenue and food to the Sultanate.

Muhammad bin Tughluq increased revenue demands in this region. The additional taxation coincided with famine and agricultural distress. Many peasants were unable to meet the demand, and the situation contributed to rebellion and resistance.

The Sultan also attempted measures to extend cultivation, including the provision of assistance or loans for agricultural development. These efforts should be distinguished from the earlier increase in taxation: they were intended to encourage cultivation, whereas the increased demand placed additional pressure on cultivators.

Comparison with Alauddin Khalji

AspectAlauddin KhaljiMuhammad bin Tughluq
Mongol policyPrimarily defensive mobilisationAlso contemplated an offensive campaign towards Transoxiana
Military accommodationBuilt the garrison town of SiriUsed Dehli-i-Kuhna for soldiers
Paying soldiersCash salariesCash salaries
Supporting financial measureRegulated market pricesExperimented with token currency
Doab policyStrengthened revenue collectionAdditional demands during severe distress

The comparison shows why similar military objectives did not necessarily produce similar economic policies.

Prelims focus

  • Daulatabad: destination of Muhammad bin Tughluq's major population and administrative transfer.
  • Transoxiana: region associated with his proposed offensive campaign.
  • Token currency: cheaper-metal coins assigned a higher monetary value.
  • Counterfeiting and distrust undermined the token-currency experiment.
  • Additional taxation and famine contributed to rebellion in the Doab.
  • Trap: Cash salaries were used by both Alauddin and Muhammad bin Tughluq; their supporting policies differed.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, Chapter 3, The Delhi Sultans, printed pp. 40–42, 2020–21 edition; NIOS, Senior Secondary History, Lesson 9, Establishment and Expansion of the Delhi Sultanate, sections on the Tughluqs, consulted 19 November 2026; IGNOU, eGyanKosh, Economy of the Delhi Sultanate, Units 19–20, sections on state revenue and agrarian policy, consulted 19 November 2026.]

title: Muhammad bin Tughluq: Military Ambition, Currency and Administrative Difficulties

body:
Agriculture as the foundation of the economy

Most people in Sultanate India lived in rural settlements and depended directly or indirectly on agriculture. Cultivators produced food for their households, supplied markets and paid revenue to rulers or their authorised officials.

The fertility of the soil, rainfall, access to water and security of the countryside affected agricultural output. Production differed greatly between regions: an irrigated tract could support more intensive cultivation than a dry or disturbed area.

Food crops and commercial crops

Important food crops included rice, wheat, millets and pulses. Cultivators also grew crops such as cotton and sugarcane, which supplied raw materials for manufacturing or commercial sale.

The growing season depended on climate and water availability:

  • Kharif crops were associated with the rainy season.
  • Rabi crops were associated with the winter growing season.

In suitable fertile and irrigated areas, farmers could grow more than 1 crop in a year. The Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta, who visited India in the 14th century, noted the productivity of Indian agriculture and the possibility of cultivating 2 crops annually in favourable areas.

This observation does not mean that every field throughout the subcontinent produced 2 harvests each year. Water availability and local conditions determined what was possible.

Wells, water-lifting devices and canals

Irrigation helped reduce dependence on seasonal rainfall. Wells, tanks and canals were used in different regions, while water-lifting devices made it possible to draw water from below ground level.

The Persian wheel

The Persian wheel, also associated with the term saqiya, was a water-lifting mechanism. An animal-powered arrangement of wheels and gears could move a series of containers that lifted water from a well and discharged it into an irrigation channel.

Such mechanisms were part of the agricultural technology used and developed during the medieval period. Their exact origins and the chronology of their spread should not be reduced to the unsupported claim that a particular Delhi Sultan invented the device.

Canal construction under the Tughluqs

The Tughluq rulers took an interest in irrigation works. Firuz Shah Tughluq (1351–1388) was particularly associated with canal construction and repair.

Canals carrying water from the Yamuna towards the region of Hisar helped extend cultivation. More reliable water supplies could make winter crops possible in areas previously dependent mainly on seasonal rainfall.

Agricultural expansion and its consequences

Expanding cultivation affected more than crop production. It could create additional villages, increase the taxable area, support larger populations and supply grain to towns and armies.

However, agricultural growth was not automatic. Wells and canals required labour and maintenance, and farmers still faced risks from drought, floods, conflict and heavy taxation.

Prelims focus

  • Kharif: rainy-season cultivation.
  • Rabi: winter-season cultivation.
  • Ibn Battuta: 14th-century traveller who described productive agriculture and double cropping in suitable areas.
  • Persian wheel: water-lifting device used for irrigation.
  • Firuz Shah Tughluq: associated with major canal works, including irrigation in the Hisar region.
  • Trap: Double cropping depended on suitable conditions and was not universal.

[NCERT, Themes in Indian History–Part II, Class 12, Chapter 5, Through the Eyes of Travellers, section 5.2, printed pp. 127–128; IGNOU, eGyanKosh, Economy of the Delhi Sultanate, Units 20 and 22, sections on agrarian production and irrigation technology, consulted 19 November 2026; IGNOU, eGyanKosh, Land Revenue, Unit 11, section on Tughluq canal irrigation, consulted 19 November 2026.]
